author.name: Royal chancery and negotiating parties
author.occupation: Collective charter negotiated under royal authority
author.biography: Magna Carta emerged from a crisis between King John and powerful opponents in 1215. It was negotiated and issued through institutions and interests, not written by a single visionary imagining modern democracy. The document addresses practical grievances about authority, justice and property. Its later readers would discover possibilities in those promises that went well beyond the interests represented in the original settlement.

hook.text: What protects you when a ruler breaks the rules?

paragraphs: A ruler makes demands; those with enough power to resist require promises in return. Magna Carta begins in that conflict, amid grievances about money, inheritance, justice and the use of royal authority.

Much of the document is specific to its medieval setting. Reading those details matters. They show whose interests had the force to become written protections and whose did not. The charter did not begin as a universal declaration of equal rights.

Its later importance grew through reuse, reinterpretation and struggles over what authority must answer to. Some clauses acquired a reach far beyond the settlement that first contained them. The distance between origin and inheritance is part of the story.
Read as both a practical bargain and a text with an extraordinary afterlife. What turns a promise made by the powerful into a restraint they cannot simply ignore?

orientation.text: This edition presents the 1215 charter. Its clauses address particular medieval grievances; later reissues and later interpretations belong to its continuing history.
